questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the sum of $\frac{n^5}{5}+\frac{n^3}{3}+\frac{7 n}{15}$ is
questions.solution:
Let the statement $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{n})$ be defined as $P(n): \frac{n^5}{5}+\frac{n^3}{3}+\frac{7 n}{15}$ is a natural number for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ :
Step I : For $\mathrm{n}=1, \mathrm{P}(1): \frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{15}=1 \in \mathrm{N}$
Hence, it is true for $\mathrm{n}=1$.
Step II : Let it is true for $n=k$,
i.e. $\frac{k^5}{5}+\frac{k^3}{3}+\frac{7 k}{15}=\lambda \in \mathbb{N}\ldots$ (i)
Step III : For $\mathrm{n}=\mathrm{k}+1$,
$\frac{(\mathrm{k}+1)^5}{5}+\frac{(\mathrm{k}+1)^3}{3}+\frac{7(\mathrm{k}+1)}{15}$
$=\frac{1}{5}\left(k^5+5 k^4+10 k^3+10 k^2+3 k+1\right)+\frac{1}{3}\left(k^3+3 k^2+3 k+1\right)+\frac{7}{15} k+\frac{7}{15}$
$=\left(\frac{k^5}{5}+\frac{k^3}{3}+\frac{7}{15} k\right)+\left(k^4+2 k^3+3 k^2+2 k\right)+\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{15}$
$=\lambda+\mathrm{k}^4+2 \mathrm{k}^3+3 \mathrm{k}^2+2 \mathrm{k}+1$ [using equation (i)]
which is a natural number, since $\lambda \mathrm{k} \in \mathrm{N}$. Therefore, $P(k+1)$ is true, when $P(k)$ is true. Hence, from the principle of mathematical induction, the statement is true for all natural numbers $\mathrm{n}$

questions.q: The maximum value of $z = 9x + 13y$ subject to constraints $2x + 3y \le 18, 2x + y \le 10, x \ge 0, y \ge 0$ is
questions.solution:
Given, constraints are$2x + 3y \le 18, 2x + y \le 10, x \ge 0, y \ge 0$.

The feasible region is $OABCO$.

Also, $z = 9x + 13y$

At $O (0,0) , z = 0$

At $A (5,0) , z = 45$

At $B (3,4) , z = 27 + 52 = 79$

At $C (0,6) , z = 78$

$∴$ Maximum value of $z$ is $79$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\mathrm{T}(k)$ be the statement $1+3+5+\ldots+(2 k-1)=k^{2}+10$ Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution: When $\mathrm{k}=1, \mathrm{LHS}=1$ but $\mathrm{RHS}=1+10=11\therefore \mathrm{T}(1)$ is not true Let $\mathrm{T}(k)$ is true. That is $$\begin{array}{l} 1+3+5+\ldots.+(2 k-1)=k^{2}+10 \\ $\text{ Now, }$ 1+3+5+\ldots..+(2 k-1)+(2 k+1) \\ =k^{2}+10+2 k+1=(k+1)^{2}+10 \end{array}$\therefore \mathrm{T}(k+1)$ is true. That is $\mathrm{T}(k)$ is true $\Rightarrow \mathrm{T}(k+1)$ is true. But $\mathrm{T}(n)$ is not true for all $n \in \mathbf{N},$ as $\mathrm{T}(1)$ is not true.
